tier_reason: First-party comparison.md with public harnesses (benchmarks/bench_engine.mojo, benchmarks/python/bench_engine.py, benchmarks/rust/src/bench_engine.rs) and tool versions, but no CPU or hardware is named, so not A; tier stays C. The headline geomean is overstated by rows where the three harnesses do different work.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page (mojo-regex 0.13.0, comparison.md): Mojo vs Python re geomean 24.54x over 76 shared benchmarks (Mojo wins 74, Python wins 1); Mojo vs Rust regex geomean 3.47x over 71 shared benchmarks (Mojo wins 59, Rust wins 11). Extreme rows: is_match_digits 1.223 ns vs Python 9.300 us (7,607x), is_match_predefined_word 1.176 ns vs 21.190 us (18,013x), wildcard_match_any 0.838 ns vs Python 4.571 us (5,454x) and Rust 38.319 us (45,718x). Excluding the 5 is_match rows and wildcard_match_any (different work, see caveats), Mojo vs Python is about 14.7x geomean over 70 rows; excluding wildcard_match_any, no_literal_baseline and alternation_common_prefix, Mojo vs Rust is about 2.6x over 68 rows (both derived from page data). Mojo loses to Python on sub_group_word_swap (1.2x slower) and to Rust on 11 rows (e.g. predefined_digits 3.6x, range_lowercase 3.8x slower).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Mojo 0.26.2 stable, default optimisation (benchmarks run with mojo run); CPython 3.12 re (build flags of the interpreter not stated); Rust regex 1.10 with Cargo profile.release opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, RUSTFLAGS -C target-cpu=native (benchmarks/rust/Cargo.toml, run_comparison_with_rust.sh). rustc version not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party, hardware not stated, so tier C. Several extreme rows compare different work: (1) the five is_match_* rows time Mojo's bool-only is_match, which can stop after the first matching character, against Python's bool(pattern.match(text)), which runs the full greedy match over a 10,000-character input (7,434x to 18,013x); (2) wildcard_match_any hits a pattern-string special case in src/regex/matcher.mojo (_is_wildcard_match_any: pattern == ".*" returns Match(0, start, len(text)) without scanning), so no regex runs; that shortcut also ignores newlines, which '.' should not match, and is only correct here because the test text has none (stb-zip/Pipa-style row, 5,454x vs Python and 45,718x vs Rust); (3) no_literal_baseline and alternation_common_prefix time Mojo match_first (one anchored match) against Rust find_iter().collect() over the whole 6,000-character text (844.7x and 177.9x). The Mojo harness has no black_box equivalent, so sub-2 ns rows are at loop-overhead level and may be partly hoisted (not confirmable without running). The Python column includes CPython interpreter call overhead (roughly 100+ ns per call), which dominates nanosecond rows, so it is not a clean measurement of the C sre engine; Rust regex is not a C/C++ baseline. The compile-time (comptime) API is not used in the comparison table. comparison.md was produced with Mojo 0.26.2 while the code now targets Mojo 1.0.0. Missing features (case-insensitive, non-greedy, word boundaries, lookaround, named groups) mean the engine supports a smaller regex language than re or Rust regex. Rows missing from one side are blank.
corrections.why_faster: Engine design, not Mojo codegen: a hybrid DFA, NFA, PikeVM, OnePass and lazy-DFA engine chosen per pattern with SIMD literal prefilters, against CPython's backtracking sre engine plus interpreter call overhead. The largest ratios come from harness differences (short-circuit is_match vs full greedy match, a '.*' pattern-string shortcut, match_first vs find_iter). The optional compile-time API (DFA built in Mojo's comptime interpreter) is not exercised by the comparison table.

notes: Numbers on comparison.md match the record exactly and the geomeans reproduce (24.54x, 3.47x). Main shortcomings: is_match rows compare short-circuit bool against Python's full greedy re.match; wildcard_match_any is a '.*' string special case that returns the whole text without running a regex and is wrong for text containing newlines; two Rust rows time findall against Mojo's single match; Python timings include interpreter overhead; no hardware. Derived geomean without those rows is about 14.7x vs Python and 2.6x vs Rust.

tier_reason: docs/compare.md is first-party; benchmark code is public (benches/check.rs and the-mikedavis/ffi-dictionaries benches/*-check.rs) but no CPU, compiler version or flags are stated, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Spellbook: cargo bench with Criterion 0.8 (benches/check.rs). Hunspell and Nuspell: vendored C++ sources compiled by the cc crate in the-mikedavis/ffi-dictionaries build.rs with no explicit opt_level or flags, nightly Rust toolchain (rust-toolchain.toml), timed with libtest #[bench]. Under cargo bench the bench profile inherits release opt-level 3, which the cc crate passes as -O3, so both sides are probably optimised at level 3 without -march (inferred from Cargo and cc defaults; not stated). No compiler versions or CPU stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers, CPU and compiler versions not stated, so tier C. The two sides use different harnesses (Criterion median vs nightly libtest #[bench]); the C++ side is called through an FFI shim (Nuspell_spell/Hunspell_spell taking a const char*) with c"word" literals, a small per-call cost. The word_with_suffix row is not apples to apples: the table labels it 'earthed' for all three, but ffi-dictionaries benches/nuspell-check.rs and hunspell-check.rs time 'earthly' (a literal stem that short-circuits on lookup), while Spellbook's benches/check.rs times 'earthed' with a comment on that difference. Not faster on every row: compound_word '20000th' 676.08 ns vs Nuspell 656.35 ns. Spellbook is mainly a rewrite of Nuspell, so the gain is from data-structure choices (hashbrown and foldhash vs Nuspell's own hash table with std::hash, compact stem and flagset representation), not Rust codegen; the author labels the string-search explanation a suspicion and did not profile. The ffi-dictionaries harness is GPL-3.0 and has 1 star. Only en_US is in the comparison table (check.rs also benches fr_FR, without a C++ comparison).
corrections.why_faster: Data structures and libraries, per the author: hashbrown's SwissTable (SIMD group probing) with foldhash for the stem multi-map where Nuspell rolls its own hash table keyed by std::hash; a compact string and slice representation with small-string and small-slice optimisations for stems and flagsets (cuts total allocation to 2.58 MB vs Nuspell 4.44 MB); the claim that Rust's standard library string search is faster is an unprofiled suspicion. Same check algorithm as Nuspell, so the win is not the language itself.

notes: All claimed numbers (check() rows and DHAT totals) match docs/compare.md. Metadata confirmed: MPL-2.0, 148 stars, last commit 2026-07-11, active. Shortcomings: no CPU or compiler versions; word_with_suffix row mixes 'earthly' (C++ benches) with 'earthed' (Spellbook bench); different harnesses; compound row not faster than Nuspell; C++ -O3 only inferred from cc crate defaults.

tier_reason: First-party article (README.md) with public Haskell code and build flags in package.yaml, but no CPU model (only '4 core 2013 Macbook Pro'), unknown build of the macOS C wc, and admittedly unscientific timing, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 543 MB plain text: wc 2.07 s vs multicore-wc 1.23 s and streaming-wc 1.07 s (about 1.7x and 1.9x faster, derived from page data). UTF-8: wc -mwl 5.56 s vs multicore-utf8-wc 3.07 s and streaming-utf-wc 2.67 s (about 1.8x and 2.1x, derived from page data). Single-core Haskell does not win: inlined-monoid-bs-wc 2.73 s vs wc 2.06 s on 543 MB, and 0.47 s vs 0.37 s on 90 MB.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Haskell: GHC via Stack resolver lts-14.1 (stack.yaml); executable built with -O2 -threaded -rtsopts -with-rtsopts=-N plus package-wide -fstatic-argument-transformation -fspec-constr-recursive=10 -funbox-strict-fields and StrictData (package.yaml at HEAD; the article itself does not state flags). C baseline: the wc binary shipped with macOS (Apple text_cmds-68 source), build flags unknown.
corrections.caveats: Author calls the timings unscientific: averages of a few runs after warming the disk cache, no confidence intervals. Baseline is the Mac's BSD-derived C wc (text_cmds-68), not GNU wc, and its build flags are unknown; the author notes faster wc implementations exist. The win comes only from parallelism: multicore-wc runs one thread per core on disjoint file ranges and streaming-wc processes 1 MB chunks in parallel with Streamly's aheadly, against single-threaded wc; multicore user time is 4.22 s vs 2.07 s wall for wc, and single-core Haskell is slower than wc. In UTF-8 mode the Haskell code counts non-continuation bytes and classifies whitespace per byte, while wc -m decodes every character through the locale, so the work differs; a later commit (2019-10-18, 'Fix up handling of space detection on UTF-8 strings') changed space detection, and the article does not say whether the UTF-8 table was re-measured after it. CPU model not given.
corrections.why_faster: Parallelism, not per-core code quality: chunked counting with a monoidal state merged across word boundaries runs on 4 cores (multicore-wc) or as parallel 1 MB stream chunks (streaming-wc), while the C wc is single-threaded; in UTF-8 mode the Haskell version also skips locale decoding. The single-threaded Haskell version is 1.3x slower than wc.

notes: All numbers match README.md (the article copy). Metadata confirmed: BSD-3-Clause, 137 stars, last commit 2021-08-20, abandoned. Shortcomings: multi-threaded Haskell vs single-threaded macOS wc of unknown build; single-core Haskell slower; UTF-8 mode does less work than wc -m; warm-cache unscientific timing; no CPU model. The 2019 post is widely known (it started a series of 'beating wc' follow-ups; general knowledge, not re-checked here), so notable despite 137 stars.
